clue.text: Deity and prince direct

blocks.note: Mars is the Roman god of war
Prince Hal, the young Henry V in Shakespeare

explanation.surface: A god and a royal heir take charge together.
explanation.walkthrough: Prince Hal is the youthful Henry V of Shakespeare's history plays, a stock crossword prince.
explanation.definitionFit: To marshal troops or people is to guide, arrange and order them, much as you would control or steer them.

clue.text: Title earned, a first in medicine secured

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept
something secured is held fast, so the outer word grips the others inside it

blocks.note: you have made money when you have earned it
taken as written
the opening letter of medicine

explanation.surface: Someone earns a title after taking a first-class degree in medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A first' reads like a top degree, but it is the article A followed by the first letter of medicine, both lodged inside MADE.
explanation.definitionFit: Madame is a French form of address for a woman, used as a courtesy title before her surname.

clue.text: Incarcerate bishop for example in robes of cardinal?

indicators.note: one thing placed within another, so these letters sit inside the outer word

blocks.note: a cardinal's robes are scarlet
a bishop is one of the men in chess

explanation.surface: A churchman is locked up while still wearing a cardinal's vestments.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the robes are described by colour, not named; a bishop is a chess piece, or man.
explanation.definitionFit: To remand an accused person is to send them back into custody to await trial, keeping them locked up.

clue.text: The fool had nuts, fruit and veg etc

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so these letters have gone wild and rearranged

blocks.note: ten letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A jester's diet of nuts, fruit and vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' sits naturally in a list of foods, but it is the signal to rearrange the three words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh produce and similar wholesome items are the typical stock of shops selling nutritious, natural eating.

clue.text: Personal details with which leader in government accesses sensitive area?

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its front, so only that one is kept
to access a place is to get inside it, so one piece enters the other

blocks.note: the opening letter of government
the loins are the delicate area around the groin

explanation.surface: A head of government gets into a secure zone using private credentials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sensitive area' suggests a classified site, but here it is a part of the body. The definition runs on into the wordplay: details with which one accesses a system.
explanation.definitionFit: A login is the username and password that a person enters to gain entry to a computer system.

clue.text: Sticker insect attached to mammal

blocks.note: a seal is a marine mammal
an ant is an insect

explanation.surface: A bug clings to the hide of a larger animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The insect comes first in the clue but last in the answer: being attached to the mammal, it follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sealant is a substance that adheres to surfaces and fills gaps, so it is something that sticks.

clue.text: Energy repeatedly drained from dignified old band

indicators.note: draining something takes it out, and doing so repeatedly removes every instance

blocks.note: statuesque means stately and dignified
E is the physics symbol for energy, here removed twice
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: An aging group of musicians has lost its old vigour.
explanation.walkthrough: Both Es come out of the longer adjective, leaving STATUSQU, and O is added. Status Quo is a long-running British rock band.
explanation.definitionFit: Status Quo are a famous British rock group, formed in the 1960s and still touring decades later.

clue.text: Wheels in a sofa bed sheared off

indicators.note: shearing trims away the edges, so the outermost letters are lost

blocks.note: taken as written
a futon is a mattress that folds into a sofa

explanation.surface: Castors on a sofa bed have been cut off.
explanation.walkthrough: The futon loses its first and last letters, leaving UTO. 'Wheels' is informal slang for a car.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheels is slang for a car, and auto is the informal American term for a motor car.

clue.text: A charger dropping tail in familiar walk

indicators.note: dropping the tail means losing the final letter
placed within, so the shortened piece sits inside the outer word

blocks.note: taken as written
a mate is a friend, someone familiar
a bull charges

explanation.surface: A warhorse that has lost its tail is taken for a gentle stroll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charger' suggests a horse, but it is a bull, which charges; minus its last letter it goes inside MATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To ambulate is a formal or medical term meaning to move about on foot, the same as walking.

clue.text: Books everyone can see wrapped in the Indian cloth

indicators.note: something wrapped in a covering lies inside it

blocks.note: THE plus SARI, the draped garment worn in India
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing

explanation.surface: Volumes on public display are bound in fabric from India.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British film classification meaning suitable for all audiences, so 'everyone can see' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Thesauri are reference volumes listing synonyms, plural of thesaurus, so they are a kind of book.

clue.text: A chevron in a figure behind curved shape, really?

indicators.note: placed within, so these letters go inside the number word
behind means coming after, so this part follows the other

blocks.note: a dome is a rounded roof
the second 'a', taken as written
a number
taken as written
a chevron is a V-shaped stripe

explanation.surface: A sergeant's stripe sits inside a shape drawn behind a curve; can that be right?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Really?' looks like a mere flourish but is the definition. The phrase is British slang meaning 'you can't be serious'.
explanation.definitionFit: Do me a favour is a sceptical British exclamation, like an incredulous 'really?' or 'come off it'.

clue.text: Permitted furniture in retirement home?

blocks.note: a playful reading: a retired person's house is gran's
a table is an item of furniture

explanation.surface: Which pieces of furniture are allowed in a care home?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the stretch: furniture found in a retiree's home is a gran table.
explanation.definitionFit: Something grantable can be allowed or conceded, so it is capable of being permitted by whoever decides.

clue.text: Tedious, anything but in the wisdom of cattle?

indicators.note: placed within, so these letters go inside the other piece

blocks.note: the sound cattle make
nous is British slang for common sense
'anything but happy' means not happy

explanation.surface: Is the intelligence of cows dull? Quite the reverse, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: The cattle's wisdom is MOO-NOUS, and NOT is placed after its first two letters. Nous is a British word for practical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Something monotonous is dull and wearisome because it never varies, which is exactly what tedious describes.

clue.text: Bone first of all in upper legs? No, arms

indicators.note: the first of all the following words means the opening letter of each one

blocks.note: initials of the four words

explanation.surface: Where is this bone located: thighs, or rather the forearm?
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pretends to correct itself about where the bone lies, and the correction is right: the bone is in the forearm.
explanation.definitionFit: The ulna is one of the two long bones of the human forearm, on the little-finger side.

clue.text: Sweat produced collecting land tax once

indicators.note: something produced has been made up anew, so the letters are reworked
to collect is to gather in, so the outer piece takes the other inside

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging
Latin for land, as in terra firma

explanation.surface: Toiling hard to gather a historic tax on land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Land tax' reads as one phrase, but the tax is the definition and the land is TERRA. Water rates were the UK household charge for water before metering.
explanation.definitionFit: Water rates were a British levy on households for water supply, so they were a tax in former times.

clue.text: Cuts of beef taken from this, say what oughta go with knife?

definitions.text: Cuts of beef taken from this

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the phrase and listen to how it comes out

blocks.note: a fork ought to go with a knife, said in a non-rhotic accent

explanation.surface: A cut of beef, and what cutlery should sit alongside the knife.
explanation.walkthrough: In a southern British accent 'fork oughta' runs together into the same sounds. The definition is a description: the region of a carcass from which several cuts come.
explanation.definitionFit: The forequarter is the front section of a beef carcass, the source of chuck, brisket and similar joints.

clue.text: A theatre fine, well set up for musical performance

indicators.note: in a down clue, setting up raises the letters so they read from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
a rep is a repertory theatre
OK means fine
cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like well!

explanation.surface: A theatre is fitted out properly to stage a musical show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well set up' looks like praise for the theatre; well is the British exclamation COR, and 'set up' turns the whole string over.
explanation.definitionFit: A rock opera is a stage or recorded work telling a story through rock songs, like Tommy, so it is a musical show.

clue.text: Acrobatic flick in roll?

indicators.note: acrobatic means tumbling and twisting, so these letters turn over into a new order
placed within, so these letters go inside the other piece

blocks.note: a bap is a soft bread roll in Britain
taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: A gymnast flips themselves over in a roll.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the move as well as giving the wordplay. A bap is a soft British bread roll.
explanation.definitionFit: A backflip is a gymnastic somersault turning backwards in the air, an athletic flick of the body in a rolling motion.

clue.text: Florist, say, arrives and rose finally pulled from wreath?

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word before it
pulling something out removes it, leaving the rest behind

blocks.note: ARR is the timetable abbreviation for arrives
the final letter of rose
taken as written; without the E it becomes wrath, a synonym of anger

explanation.surface: A florist turns up, and the last rose is plucked from a funeral garland.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking E out of WREATH leaves WRATH, which must then be swapped for its synonym ANGER to join ARR.
explanation.definitionFit: A florist is one example of someone who arranges things, in this case composing displays of cut flowers.

clue.text: In this, leader flies solo round outskirts of Chile?

definitions.text: In this, leader flies solo round outskirts of Chile?

indicators.note: the outskirts of a place are its edges, so the outer letters are kept
going round something encloses it, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: to fly is to travel by air
solo means for one person
the first and last letters of Chile

explanation.surface: A president travels alone, circling the edges of a South American country.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes the US presidential aircraft with the leader aboard; 'flies solo' splits into travel by air and for one person.
explanation.definitionFit: Air Force One is the call sign of the aircraft carrying the President of the United States, the leader who travels aboard.

clue.text: Indication in slang I screwed up

indicators.note: something screwed up is crumpled or botched, so the letters end up jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written; that the letters also run backwards across these words is a coincidence

explanation.surface: A sign, expressed in slang, that I made a mess of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screwed up' is itself slang, so it reads as an example of what the clue describes.
explanation.definitionFit: A signal is a sign or gesture that conveys information, which is what an indication does.

clue.text: See 9 Across
Question posed by Buddhist, right out of holy book

indicators.note: out of means taken away from, so a letter goes missing

blocks.note: the Koran is the holy book of Islam
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A Buddhist poses a puzzle, though the right answer is missing from the scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: The holy book is Islamic, which jars with the Buddhist surface; removing R from it leaves the Zen term.
explanation.definitionFit: A koan is a paradoxical riddle set by a Zen master to a student to provoke insight beyond logic.

clue.text: One gets squeezed in front of carriage as soon as train moves

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter
when letters move about they settle in a new order

blocks.note: the opening letter of carriage
'once you arrive' means as soon as you arrive
taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: A passenger is crushed in the first carriage the moment the train sets off.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a packed commuter train; the definition is the instrument, which is squeezed to play.
explanation.definitionFit: A concertina is a small bellows instrument played by compressing and expanding it between the hands.

clue.text: Person encrypting information ending on the radio?

indicators.note: what is on the radio is heard, not seen, so we go by sound

blocks.note: a coda is the closing section of a piece of music

explanation.surface: A cryptographer sends out the conclusion of a message by wireless.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent the final R is silent, so the two words sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A coder converts messages into code, which is what someone encrypting data does to keep it secret.

clue.text: Label cut for breakfast food

indicators.note: cutting trims something short, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: a trade label

explanation.surface: A manufacturer trims the label on a cereal box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' could be read as the definition, but it shortens the label by its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Bran is the husk of cereal grain, eaten as flakes or added to muesli in the morning.

clue.text: Designer range of beers with one exported?

indicators.note: exported goods are sent away, so this letter leaves

blocks.note: lager is a type of beer
a range, as in a field of vision
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A designer line of beers is sold overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: A range of beers is a lager field; sending away I leaves the surname of Karl Lagerfeld, the German fashion designer behind Chanel.
explanation.definitionFit: Karl Lagerfeld was a German couturier, long the creative director of Chanel and Fendi.

clue.text: Smack heel in disco dance

indicators.note: the heel is the back end of a foot, so the last letter is kept

blocks.note: a smack is a taste or flavour
the final letter of disco

explanation.surface: A heel strike while dancing at a disco.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smack' suggests a blow, but it is the noun for a taste, as in a smack of garlic.
explanation.definitionFit: The tango is a ballroom dance from Argentina, with sharp steps and close holds between partners.

clue.text: Stripper managed to break a joint, bending backwards

indicators.note: bending back turns something the other way, so the letters run right to left
breaking into something gets inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
the hip is a joint
to run a business is to manage it

explanation.surface: An exotic dancer contorts herself backwards and puts a hip out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripper' suggests a dancer, but the fish strips flesh from its prey.
explanation.definitionFit: Piranhas are flesh-eating South American fish whose shoals can strip an animal to the bone.

clue.text: Criminal taking the lower street, one going straight on the outside?

indicators.note: something on the outside wraps around whatever lies within

blocks.note: a ruler keeps a line straight
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A crook takes a lower road, while a reformed one stays outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The lower' is a cow, something that lows, and a cattle thief takes it. 'One going straight' sounds like a reformed crook but is a ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: A rustler steals livestock, so he is a criminal who makes off with cattle, the animals that moo.
